# PPortal

> PlayStation Remote Play for Windows, built on .NET 10 and WPF. Ten-bit video composed by
> DirectComposition, hardware decode chosen from what the machine reports, the consoles and
> pairings you already registered, and no browser inside the download.

Site: https://alegauss.github.io/pportal/
Source: https://github.com/alegauss/pportal
Licence: AGPL-3.0
Platform: Windows 10 or 11, x64. There is no Linux, macOS, Android or Switch build, and
that is a decision rather than a gap.

Every page on this site has a Markdown twin at the same address with `index.md` appended,
converted from the same render as the HTML, so it cannot disagree with the page. The list
of routes, their twins and their sizes is in `manifest.json`.

## What it is

A remote play client that behaves like a Windows program. The streaming protocol comes
from the Chiaki and chiaki-ng projects; what PPortal rebuilt is everything around it: the
window, the video presentation, the input path and the settings, on .NET rather than Qt.

## The video path

- The decoded frame never goes through WPF's own image path, which accepts eight bits per
  channel and nothing wider, so HDR would be ruled out before the stream started.
- libplacebo renders into a shared Direct3D 11 texture, and DirectComposition puts that
  texture on screen as a ten-bit plane with the window's overlay composed above it.
- The overlay is above the plane rather than behind it, because that is the one arrangement
  of the three that keeps both the ten-bit picture and the stream HUD.
- The present is paced by the refresh rate of the display the window is on, and a rate
  change mid-session changes the pacing with it.
- libplacebo's scalers, debanding, tone curves and colour mapping are exposed on two
  screens, with presets over the sliders.

## Decode, and what a machine without an NVIDIA card keeps

- d3d11va, Vulkan and CUDA are the decode paths. CUDA is preferred only when the window
  reports an NVIDIA card and the decoder is actually available; otherwise Vulkan, then
  d3d11va.
- The floor on a machine with no NVIDIA card: hardware decode through d3d11va, a renderer
  that is Vulkan with an OpenGL fallback, and an SDR present that loads nothing from NVIDIA.
- A feature that is not available is not in the menu. There is no dialog explaining that a
  different card would be better.
- The measurements published for this project were taken on an RTX 4060, and every recorded
  result names the card. Paced at 60fps, the CUDA path measured last of the three.

## Input

- Directional focus navigation on every screen, attached to ordinary WPF controls rather
  than built into a private set of lookalike widgets.
- SDL owns the device list, the button events and the axis positions, read on the thread
  that owns it, so a pad plugged in mid-session works.
- The mapping screen reads the device's own binding strings and captures a press against
  the slot you picked.
- Keyboard bindings are a tab in the settings.

## The screens

- The console list is the front door: discovery, manual hosts and hidden consoles in one
  list, with each row offering what its state allows (stream, wake, or retry).
- Registration is one dialog on its own path and three more reached from elsewhere, and the
  PIN rules for the two console generations are kept as two rules.
- Settings are nine tabs: General, Video, Stream, Audio, Consoles, Keys, Controllers,
  Remote and Config, committed when a field is finished.
- Where a stored value is not the label shown, the stored value stayed, so a setting reads
  back the way it always did.
- Signing in to PSN runs in a WebView2 panel on the runtime Windows already carries, so
  there is no second browser in the download.

## What it records

- Each session appends one line to a record on the local machine, naming the decoder, the
  renderer, the requested bitrate and both loss settings.
- Timed per session: receive, reorder dwell, reassemble, error correction, and the decoder's
  send-to-pull.
- A latency floor: input queueing plus the console's own reported round trip, in
  milliseconds.
- `compare-baselines` reads two records and prints p50, p99 and maximum per stage with the
  difference, and refuses two records whose field sets differ.
- Nothing is uploaded. There is no account anywhere in the application.

## Setup

- Registered consoles, manual and hidden hosts, controller mappings and the PSN token are
  read from the store already on the machine, resolved against the active Windows profile.
- The installer uses an identifier of its own, so an existing chiaki-ng installation is left
  in place rather than upgraded, and both can be run on the same machine.

## Non-goals

- No Linux, macOS, Android or Switch build.
- No cross-platform UI toolkit, because it would give back none of the Win32, DXGI and
  WebView2 access the screens and the video path depend on.
- No vendor path whose absence is visible to the user.
- No redesign of screens that already worked.
- No telemetry.

## Pages

- / : the landing page
- /features/picture/ : the video path, and why the overlay sits above the plane
- /features/controllers/ : focus navigation, SDL, and the mapping capture
- /features/screens/ : the console list, the dialogs, and the nine settings tabs
- /features/latency/ : what is timed, and how two runs are compared
- /features/setup/ : what comes across from an existing installation
- /hardware/ : what this asks of your GPU, and the floor without an NVIDIA card
